narrative: The model estimated a 60% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because that is more likely than not, your law school application was denied. Your gender and race were not used; the decision reflects the academic pattern in the information reviewed. The strongest factor was your law school admission test score. Your score of 40 was above the average of 37.18 among accepted students, so this factor actually pushed the prediction toward passing. The second most important factor was your undergraduate GPA. At 2.50, it was well below the accepted-student average of 3.23, and this pushed the prediction toward failure. The third factor was your third-year class-rank decile. Your decile of 3 was much lower than the accepted-student average of 5.79, and this also pushed toward failure. In other words, your admission test result was a protective strength, but the concerns tied to your undergraduate record and third-year academic standing together outweighed it. To strengthen a future application, focus on addressing the academic concerns directly: consider additional coursework or a post-baccalaureate record that demonstrates readiness, seek advising about your third-year performance, and discuss any extenuating circumstances through the appropriate application process. You may also consider retaking the admission test only if practice results show meaningful improvement, and plan for structured bar-exam preparation before enrollment.
